messages.author: fc3bad353a026ca0
messages.subject: unexpected grouping behavior
parts:
Could someone help me understand why the following code does not
create 4 separate lines?

a<-seq(from=-pi, to=pi, by=pi/4)
x=rep(a,4)
y=c(sin(a), sin(a)+.2, sin(a)+.4, sin(a)+.6)
sample=rep(1:2, each=9, times=2)
origin=rep(1:2, each=18)

df<-data.frame(x, y, sample, origin)
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, color=factor(origin), group=factor(sample)))
+ geom_path()

messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: Re: unexpected grouping behavior
parts:
Well

1) You only have two levels in your grouping factor, so that is all
you will get, but
2) It does create 4 lines, two are distinguished by shape, two by
colour, which is exactly what you asked for (though perhaps not what
you want).

I get the feeling you are angling for:

ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, group=interaction(factor(origin), factor(sample)))) +
geom_path()

which as the grouping variable passes the interaction of origin and
sample. You are free to colour as you please.

HTH,

Josh

messages.author: fc3bad353a026ca0
messages.subject: Re: unexpected grouping behavior
parts:
Thanks, I didn't know that you could use interaction() with group.
That solves my problem.

Knowing that, the graph I wanted to create is:
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, group=interaction(factor(origin),
factor(sample)), color=factor(origin))) +
geom_path()

Seems strange that my original code created 2 separate lines:

ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, color=factor(origin), group=factor(sample)))
+
geom_path()

but this creates 4 separate lines:
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, color=factor(origin),
linetype=factor(sample))) +
geom_path()

Thanks,
Ian

messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Re: unexpected grouping behavior
parts:
ian,

The reason for the difference is that, by default, group is set to the
interaction of all the other aesthetic factors. So in your second
example, there is an implicit
group=interaction(factor(origin),factor(sample)) since one is used for
color and one for linetype. In the first example, you override the
default group specification (factor(origin)) with a different one
(factor(sample)).

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University
